Pop in your mint usb and restart the computer. A Mint menu will show up. Both "install mint" and "try mint without installing" are useful directions to go and you can install mint from both. I personally always pick the try without installing. In fact do that.

Click the start menu in mint. Open up gparted by beginning to type it. Use it to make a 2gig swap and the rest ext4 from the empty space you got working in windows. The ext4 is where linux will go so the size of your windows ntfs and your linux ext4 depends on how big you want them to be.

Now click the "install mint" on the desktop. Every option in there is a sane default. The only one I select something other than the default is at the menu that gives you an option of "replace windows", "install mint along side windows", I always select "do something else" just so I can do it manually.

Only one action is need in the "do something else" menu. Click on the ext4 you made at set its mount point to "/" without quotes.

This is hopefully what "install mint alongside windows" would do but I like to make sure.

That's it. Continue on with any other options, you can't fuck up.

Only 5? I could probably rattle 10 off the top of my head.

1. Free (as in money)
  2. Free (as in freedom)
  3. Customizable/highly flexible
  4. More secure and private
  5. Fully-integrated gloat factor

It's sad but as an IT guy who enjoys learning and PCs, I can't dedicate myself to Linux. It's specifically because of #3.

Highly flexible and customizable also means easy to break if you don't know what you are doing. They just go hand in hand.

My Windows install breaks from time to time. When it does, I can usually fix the issue and it gets back to working.

Every time I've tried a Linux installation, I follow a guide to fix an issue when they inevitably come up (they do with all installations for me) and it usually fixes it. But then I do that a few times over the lifespan of an OS install and I end up breaking something that I don't remember how to fix originally and I'm stuck with a broken OS.

I am prone to these issues specifically because I like customizing things. I like having special features and stuff like it.

The problem is that I don't have a full understanding of everything in a Linux system. So when I customize one thing, and another thing breaks that's related to or relies on the thing I customized, say adding Samba/CIFS support to a Linux install and then for some reason my ZFS drives won't import like they are supposed to on boot (it's not as simple as editing the /etc/fstab), there isn't a simple guide for fixing the issue because it's related to another customization I did which makes my system unique.

I've tried Ubuntu, Debian, and I'm currently using LXLE on a flash drive for trouble shooting and such on client PCs.

I don't know. Every time I've had a Linux install, I eventually went back to Windows because it ended up broken for whatever reason.

I spend enough time fixing my own computer and I use Windows as it is. I don't have enough time to fix it more once it's Linux (which is my fault, not Linux's) and relearn an OS on top of that.

I'm trying to learn it as I go, but I don't know if I'll ever be proficient enough to fix the intricate issues I self-create by being a special snowflake in Linux well enough to dedicate myself to it as my main OS.
